extracted.intended_audience: political thinkers, legislators, and an educated public concerned with governance (late-18th-century British readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical essay analysing the constitutional, military, municipal, and financial consequences of the French Revolution; it offers normative judgments about how armies, municipalities, officers, and revenue should be organized. The text is addressed to legislators and citizens concerned with the stability of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army should act only as an instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: "The nature of things requires that the army should never act but as an instrument."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The army must not erect itself into a deliberate body acting by its own resolutions; if it does, the government will degenerate into a 'military democracy' that ultimately devours its creators. Maintain the army's role strictly as an instrument of civil authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit irregular soldier committees and consultations
rubrics_metrics.description: Against "irregular consultations and turbulent committees formed in some regiments by the common soldiers and non-commissioned officers... monstrous democratic assemblies [comices]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such assemblies, especially when formed without the knowledge or in contempt of superiors, undermine discipline and are politically dangerous. Presence and concurrence of superiors is required; encourage strict suppression of soldier-formed political committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit municipal authority over troops to requisition
rubrics_metrics.description: You have bounded the action which you have permitted to the latter over the former to the right of requisition; but never did the letter or the spirit of your decrees authorize the commons in these municipalities to break the officers, to try them, to give orders to the soldiers, to drive them from the posts... or, in a word, to enslave the troops to the caprice of each of the cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Municipalities must not be permitted to exercise disciplinary or command powers over national troops. Civil authorities' lawful interaction with military forces should be narrowly circumscribed to requisition and support, not command or trial of officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attempt to restore military obedience by civilian fraternization
rubrics_metrics.description: The king... has promulgated... that the several corps should join themselves with the clubs and confederations in the several municipalities, and mix with them in their feasts and civic entertainments!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing soldiers into municipal clubs, civic feasts, and convivial societies ('jolly discipline') is unlikely to restore obedience to officers or teach military discipline; it may produce better citizens 'after the French mode' but worse soldiers. Civic swearing, clubbing, and feasting cannot substitute for military command and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers' appointment and promotion must preserve chain of command
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisional nomination of the officers... to the king, with a reserve of approbation by the National Assembly... this double negotiation for military rank seems... as if it were studied... to promote faction in the Assembly itself relative to this vast military patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid systems where officers must seek patronage or approval from competing political bodies; double sources of appointment (court and Assembly) encourage faction and politicization of the officer corps. Promotion rules should reduce incentives for officers to pursue political intrigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army requires a real, vigorous, personal authority at its head
rubrics_metrics.description: They must be constrained... by a real, vigorous, effective, decided, personal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nominal or captive head of the army (a 'cipher') cannot effectively command; the supreme command requires a single, decisive personal authority to secure obedience and prevent the ascendancy of a populist general who could dominate the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve officers as primary focus of soldiers' loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure a real army, the officer should be first and last in the eye of the soldier,--first and last in his attention, observance, and esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military order depends on the officer being unquestioned as the soldiers' primary object of loyalty. Electioneering arts, treating officers as candidates rather than commanders, or providing soldiers power to cashier officers corrodes this primacy and undermines discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching soldiers political rights that conflict with military duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The soldier is told he is a citizen, and has the rights of man and citizen... he will... exercise at least a negative in the choice of his officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political doctrines that emphasize individual civic rights to soldiers (e.g., rights to elect or judge officers) weaken military subordination. Legislators should refrain from inculcating civic doctrines in ways that encourage soldiers to substitute political judgment for military obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal (national guard) forces must not replace coherent national military structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The municipal army... is a mere democratic body, unconnected with the crown or the kingdom, armed and trained and officered at the pleasure of the districts... If... considered in any relation to the crown, to the National Assembly, to the public tribunals, or to the other army... it seems a monster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locally controlled, elective municipal forces may be uniform in themselves but become dangerous when related to national institutions; such forces can fragment authority, encourage local sovereignty, and endanger national cohesion. Coherence between parts of the military and central authority is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't rely solely on military coercion as the instrument of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything depends upon the army in such a government as yours; for you have industriously destroyed all the opinions and prejudices... Therefore the moment any difference arises between your National Assembly and any part of the nation, you must have recourse to force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A polity that systematically undermines civil authority and habits of subordination leaves itself dependent on armed coercion. Legislators should foster institutions and opinions that make force a last, not first, resort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of a finance minister / principles of public finance
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of a financier are, then, to secure an ample revenue; to impose it with judgment and equality; to employ it economically; and when necessity obliges him to make use of credit, to secure its foundations in that instance, and forever, by the clearness and candor of his proceedings, the exactness of his calculations, and the solidity of his funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public finance requires: (1) securing sufficient revenue, (2) imposing taxes with judgment and equality, (3) economical expenditure, and (4) when borrowing, ensuring transparency, accurate accounting, and sound funding. These are the practical tests of financial skill and patriotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue is the foundation of state power and public virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Through the revenue alone the body politic can act in its true genius and character... the revenue... becomes in its administration the sphere of every active virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A state's capacity for magnanimity, beneficence, defense, and reform depends on adequate and well-administered revenue. Fiscal arrangements shape the scope for public virtue and the performance of government functions.
